name: 1-Testosterone (1-Test / dihydroboldenone)
lead: 1-Testosterone (1-Test, 1-T, dihydroboldenone, DHB) is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid that was sold online in the early 2000s as a muscle-building supplement. People who used it, and the companies that marketed it, were after the same outcome as with other androgens: more lean mass, lower body fat and a fuller, harder-looking physique [1][2][3].

Chemically it is a 5-alpha-reduced derivative of boldenone and a relative of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), differing from testosterone by a double bond at the 1(2) position instead of the 4(5) position [1]. It was marketed in a supplement category known as prohormones or designer steroids, alongside compounds such as 1-androstenediol and 1-androstenedione (1-AD), which were sold as precursors that the body converts into 1-testosterone [1][3][4].

It was legally sold in the United States until 2005, when the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004 took effect and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) listed it in Schedule III under the name 1-dihydrotestosterone, or "1-testosterone" [1][5]. The only published pharmacology is a 2006 animal study; no human clinical trial of the compound has been published [1].

chain: Androgen-sensitive muscle tissue grows in animal tests
Users sought more lean mass and a fuller physique
angle.text: 1-Testosterone was marketed to people wanting to build muscle. The only published pharmacology is an animal study in which it grew the levator ani muscle about as much as testosterone propionate did.

infobox: Schedule III since 2005 (listed as "1-testosterone" in the 2004 Act) [1][5]

paras: Anabolic-androgenic steroids as a class are used for physique more than for sport: reference summaries say most non-medical users are non-competitive bodybuilders or non-athletes, typically men, and a 2020 review in the British Journal of Pharmacology described such use as largely driven by the desire for a more muscular appearance [6][7]. 1-Testosterone entered that market as a non-prescription product, sold in the era when prohormones could be bought as dietary supplements.

The supplement-era appeal of the 1-series compounds, as described by bodybuilding writers, was that they were said not to convert to estrogen or to DHT, the hormones linked to side effects such as water retention, acne, male-pattern hair loss and prostate enlargement [4]. Wikipedia lists no brand names or approved medical use for 1-testosterone and no human data [1].

1-Testosterone is a derivative of dihydrotestosterone with a double bond between carbons 1 and 2 of the A ring. It is also described as the 5-alpha-reduced form of boldenone [1]. Its prohormone forms include 1-androstenediol and 1-androstenedione, and a 2006 paper in Steroids described a synthesis of 1-androstenedione from stanolone acetate [1].

Bodybuilding writer coverage credits the supplement chemist Patrick Arnold with introducing 1-AD, and describes his earlier work on delivery systems intended to bypass first-pass liver metabolism [4].

A 2006 study by Friedel and colleagues in Toxicology Letters reported that 1-testosterone has high androgenic and anabolic potency without prior metabolism, with highly selective androgen-receptor binding and strong receptor-dependent transactivation, so that it can be considered a typical anabolic steroid [1]. In animals, an equimolar dose matched testosterone propionate in stimulating growth of the prostate, seminal vesicles and the androgen-sensitive levator ani muscle. Unlike testosterone propionate, it also increased liver weight [1].
The study used animals only [1]. Wikipedia's page lists liver metabolism and urinary excretion for the compound but gives no pharmacokinetic detail [1].

Prohormone supplements, from DHEA through androstenedione to later cyclodextrin and transdermal products, were sold over the counter after the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, according to a bodybuilding magazine history [4]. The 1990 Anabolic Steroid Control Act had placed anabolic steroids in Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act [8]. The 2004 Act, signed on 22 October 2004 and effective 20 January 2005, replaced the statutory definition of an anabolic steroid with a list of 59 named substances, including steroid metabolic precursors [5][8].

The DEA's final rule, published 16 December 2005 and effective 17 January 2006, lists Delta-1-dihydrotestosterone, "1-testosterone", and 17-alpha-methyl-1-testosterone among them [5]. Prohormone entries on Wikipedia note that androstenedione and androstenediol were also banned under the 2004 Act, and that some prohibited prohormones continued to be sold under different names [3]. A later statute, the Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2014, expanded the DEA-regulated list by about two dozen substances and created crimes for falsely labelling steroid products [8].

Reference sources note that many countries lack general analogue laws, so slightly modified steroid structures have at times fallen outside existing bans, while others, such as Australia, regulate by chemical structure [2]. Anabolic steroids are Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and Schedule IV in Canada [7].

No human adverse-event data are published for 1-testosterone itself. In the 2006 animal study it increased liver weight where testosterone propionate did not [1]. For anabolic steroids as a class, reference summaries describe cholesterol changes (higher LDL, lower HDL), hypertension, suppression of the body's own testosterone production with reduced sperm production, gynecomastia with aromatizable compounds, and liver effects mostly with 17-alpha-alkylated oral compounds [7]. Wikipedia's prohormone article lists acne, hair loss, heart-disease risk, kidney and liver dysfunction, hypertension and impotence among adverse effects of prohormones and notes that research on most prohormones is limited [3].

Quality problems have also been reported. A bodybuilding magazine analysis said a commercial 1-AD product contained boldenone and other prohormones, and that a product sold as "1-T Matrix" contained metandienone [4]. Products sold under 1-series names therefore did not always contain what the label stated, according to that source.

No studies found on 1-testosterone in people. The animal work above is the main published pharmacology [1]. A 2014 randomized trial in Journal of Applied Physiology examined a related 1-ene prohormone, 3-beta-hydroxy-5-alpha-androst-1-en-17-one, in 17 resistance-trained men over four weeks of training. The prohormone group gained more lean mass, lost more fat and improved squat and total strength more than the placebo group, and also showed lower HDL cholesterol, higher LDL cholesterol and signs of liver and kidney strain; the authors concluded the harm outweighed any benefit for that supplement [9]. This was a different compound from 1-testosterone.

Use can be detected in urine by gas chromatography, according to a 2005 case study cited by Wikipedia [1]. The bodybuilding article cited above also described contaminated 1-AD products producing positive tests for boldenone and nandrolone metabolites [4].

timeline.event: Anabolic Steroid Control Act places anabolic steroids in Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act [8].
Dietary supplement legislation allows prohormones to be sold over the counter [4].
Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004 is signed, listing 1-testosterone among 59 substances [5].
The 2004 Act takes effect; 1-testosterone is no longer legally sold [1][5].
DEA publishes the final rule implementing the Act, effective 17 January 2006 [5].
Friedel and colleagues publish an animal study of 1-testosterone's androgenic and anabolic potency [1].
Granados and colleagues publish a randomized trial of a related 1-ene prohormone [9]; the Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2014 passes the House [8].

lore.intro: Claims about the 1-series compounds circulated mostly in bodybuilding magazines and supplement marketing in the 2000s rather than in looksmaxxing forums [4].

claims.claim: 1-Test builds lean muscle comparably to testosterone.
claims.believers: Marketers and bodybuilding writers rated the 1-series among the strongest over-the-counter prohormones of their time [4].
claims.experts: A 2006 animal study found equimolar potency comparable to testosterone propionate in androgen-sensitive tissues; no human trial of 1-testosterone exists [1].

claims.claim: It does not convert to estrogen or DHT, so it avoids the usual side effects.
claims.believers: Supplement writers said the 1-series avoided estrogen- and DHT-related effects such as acne, hair loss and prostate enlargement [4].
claims.experts: Anabolic steroids as a class are linked to cholesterol, hormonal and liver effects [7], and the 2006 study saw increased liver weight in animals [1].

claims.claim: It is a legal prohormone supplement.
claims.believers: Before 2005 it was sold online as a supplement [1].
claims.experts: The 2004 Act and DEA's 2005 rule list it by name as a Schedule III anabolic steroid [5].

claims.claim: Products labelled 1-AD or 1-T contain what they say.
claims.believers: Supplement companies marketed products under the 1-series names [4].
claims.experts: A bodybuilding magazine analysis reported products containing boldenone, other prohormones or metandienone [4].

card.summary: A DHT-derived designer steroid once sold online as a supplement; controlled in the US since 2005 and untested in human trials.
card.note: Controlled substance in the US; animal data only.

quick.overview:
1-Testosterone is a synthetic androgen sold in the past as a muscle-building prohormone.

Only animal data and doping-detection literature are described; no human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor selectively, and an animal study reported potency comparable to testosterone propionate in androgen-sensitive tissues.
quick.risks: In the animal study it also increased liver weight. It has been a US Schedule III substance since 2005.
